sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen16607" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="49" osisID="Isa.49" sID="Isa.49"/> <div eID="gen16607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16608" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16609" type="x-p"/> Glorious things had been spoken in the previous chapters concerning the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon; but lest any should think, when it was accomplished, that it looked much greater and brighter in the prophecy than in the performance, and that the return of about 40,000 Jews in a poor condition out of Babylon to Jerusalem was not an event sufficiently answering to the height and grandeur of the expressions used in the prophecy, he here comes to show that the prophecy had a further intention, and was to have its full accomplishment in a redemption that should as far outdo these expressions as the other seemed to come short of them, even the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ, of whom not only Cyrus, who was God's servant in foretelling it, was a type. In this chapter we have, I. The designation of Christ, under the type of Isaiah, to his office as Mediator, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1-Isa.49.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The assurance given him of the success of his undertaking among the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4-Isa.49.8">ver. 4-8</reference>. III. The redemption that should be wrought by him, and the progress of that redemption, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.9-Isa.49.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. IV. The encouragement given hence to the afflicted church, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.13-Isa.49.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. V. The addition of many to it, and the setting up of a church among the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.18-Isa.49.23">ver. 18-23</reference>. VI. A ratification of the prophecy of the Jews' release out of Babylon, which was to be the figure and type of all these blessings,, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.24-Isa.49.26">ver. 24-26</reference>. If this chapter be rightly understood, we shall see ourselves to be more concerned in the prophecies relating to the Jews' deliverance out of Babylon than we thought we were.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me; <hi type="super">3</hi> And said unto me, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> surely my judgment <hi type="italic">is</hi> with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and my work with my God. <hi type="super">5</hi> And now, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that formed me from the womb <hi type="italic">to be</hi> his servant, to bring Jacob again to him, Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and my God shall be my strength. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth. <div eID="gen16610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16611" type="x-p"/> Here, I. An auditory is summoned together and attention demanded. The sermon in the foregoing chapter was directed to the house of Jacob and the people of Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.12">12</reference>. But this is directed to the isles (that is, the Gentiles, for they are called <hi type="italic">the isles of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen. x. 5</reference>) and to <hi type="italic">the people from far,</hi> that were <hi type="italic">strangers to the commonwealth of Israel,</hi> and afar off. Let these listen (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">v. 1</reference>) as to a thing at a distance, which yet they are to hear with desire and attention. Note, 1. The tidings of a Redeemer are sent to the Gentiles, and to those that lie most remote; and they are concerned to listen to them. 2. The Gentiles listened to the gospel when the Jews were deaf to it. <div eID="gen16611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16612" type="x-p"/> II. The great author and publisher of the redemption produces his authority from heaven for the work he had undertaken. 1. God had appointed him and set him apart for it: <hi type="italic">The Lord has called me from the womb</hi> to this office and <hi type="italic">made mention of my name,</hi> nominated me to be the Saviour. By an angel he called him <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour,</hi> who <hi type="italic">should save his people from their sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Matt. i. 21</reference>. Nay, from the womb of the divine counsels, before all worlds, he was called to this service, and help was laid upon him; and he came at the call, for he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> with an eye to what was written of him <hi type="italic">in the volume of the book.</hi> This was said of some of the prophets, as types of him, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jer. i. 5</reference>. Paul was separated to the apostleship from his mother's womb, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15">Gal. i. 15</reference>. 2. God had fitted and qualified him for the service to which he designed him. He <hi type="italic">made his mouth like a sharp sword,</hi> and <hi type="italic">made him</hi> like <hi type="italic">a polished shaft,</hi> or a bright arrow, furnished him with every thing necessary to fight God's battles against the powers of darkness, to conquer Satan, and bring back God's revolted subjects to their allegiance, by his word: that is the <hi type="italic">two-edged sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>) which comes out of his mouth, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Rev. xix. 15</reference>. The convictions of the word are the arrows that shall be sharp in the hearts of sinners, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">Ps. xlv. 5</reference>. 3. God had preferred him to the service for which he had reserved him: <hi type="italic">He has hidden me in the shadow of his hand</hi> and in his quiver, which denotes, (1.) Concealment. The gospel of Christ, and the calling in of the Gentiles by it, were long hidden from ages and generations, hidden in God (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Eph. iii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Rom. xvi. 25</reference>), hidden in the shadow of the ceremonial law and the Old-Testament types. (2.) Protection. The house of David was the particular care of the divine Providence, because that blessing was in it. Christ in his infancy was sheltered from the rage of Herod. 4. God had owned him, had said unto him, "<hi type="italic">Thou art my servant,</hi> whom I have employed and will prosper; thou art Israel, in effect, <hi type="italic">the prince with God,</hi> that hast wrestled and prevailed; and in thee I will be glorified." The people of God are <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> and they are all gathered together, summed up, as it were, in Christ, the great representative of all Israel, as the high priest who had the names of all the tribes on his breastplate; and in him God is and will be glorified; so he said by a voice from heaven, <reference osisRef="John.12.27-John.12.28">John xii. 27, 28</reference>. Some read the words in two clauses: <hi type="italic">Thou art my servant</hi> (so Christ is, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">ch. xlii. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">it is Israel in whom I will be glorified by thee;</hi> it is the spiritual Israel, the elect, in the salvation of whom by Jesus Christ God will be glorified, and his free grace for ever admired. <div eID="gen16612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16613" type="x-p"/> III. He is assured of the good success of his undertaking; for whom God calls he will prosper. And as to this, <div eID="gen16613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16614" type="x-p"/> 1. He objects the discouragement he had met with at his first setting out (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">v. 4</reference>): "Then I said, with a sad heart, <hi type="italic">I have laboured in vain;</hi> those that were ignorant, and careless, and strangers to God, are so still: <hi type="italic">I have called, and they have refused;</hi> I have <hi type="italic">stretched out my hands to a gainsaying people.</hi>" This was Isaiah's complaint, but it was no more than he was told to expect, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">ch. vi. 9</reference>. The same was a temptation to Jeremiah to resolve he would labour no more, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer. xx. 9</reference>. It is the complaint of many a faithful minister, that has not loitered, but laboured, not spared, but spent, his strength, and himself with it, and yet, as to many, it is all in vain and for nought; they will not be prevailed with to repent and believe. But here it seems to point at the obstinacy of the Jews, among whom Christ went in person preaching the gospel of the kingdom, laboured and spent his strength, and yet the rulers and the body of the nation rejected him and his doctrine; so very few were brought in, when one would think none should have stood out, that he might well say, "<hi type="italic">I have laboured in vain,</hi> preached so many sermons, wrought so many miracles, in vain." Let not the ministers think it strange that they are slighted when the Master himself was. <div eID="gen16614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16615" type="x-p"/> 2. He comforts himself under this discouragement with this consideration, that it was the cause of God in which he was engaged and the call of God that engaged him in it: <hi type="italic">Yet surely my judgment is with the Lord,</hi> who is the Judge of all, <hi type="italic">and my work with my God,</hi> whose servant I am. His comfort is, and it may be the comfort of all faithful ministers, when they see little success of their labours, (1.) That, however it be, it is a righteous cause that they are pleading. They are with God, and for God; they are on his side, and workers together with him. They like not their judgment, the rule they go by, nor their work, the business they are employed in, ever the worse for this. The unbelief of men gives them no cause to suspect the truth of their doctrine, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.3">Rom. iii. 3</reference>. (2.) That their management of this cause, and their prosecution of this work, were known to God, and they could appeal to him concerning their sincerity, and that it was not through any neglect of theirs that they laboured in vain. "<hi type="italic">He knows the way that I take; my judgment is with the Lord,</hi> to determine whether I have not delivered my soul and left the blood of those that perish on their own heads." (3.) Though the labour be in vain as to those that are laboured with, yet not as to the labourer himself, if he be faithful: his judgment is with the Lord, who will justify him and bear him out, though men condemn him and run him down; and his work (the reward of his work) is with his God, who will take care he shall be no loser, no, not by his lost labour. (4.) Though the judgment be not yet brought forth unto victory, nor the work to perfection, yet both are with the Lord, to carry them on and give them success, according to his purpose, in his own way and time. <div eID="gen16615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16616" type="x-p"/> 3. He receives from God a further answer to this objection, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5-Isa.49.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. He knew very well that God had set him on work, had <hi type="italic">formed him from the womb to be his servant,</hi> had not only called him so early to it (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">v. 1</reference>), but begun so early to fit him for it and dispose him to it. Those whom God designs to employ as his servants he is fashioning and preparing to be so long before, when perhaps neither themselves nor others are aware of it. It is he that forms the spirit of man within him. Christ was to be <hi type="italic">his servant, to bring Jacob again to him,</hi> that had treacherously departed from him. The seed of Jacob therefore, according to the flesh, must first be dealt with, and means used to bring them back. Christ, and the word of salvation by him, are sent to them first; nay, Christ comes in person to them only, <hi type="italic">to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.</hi> But what if Jacob will not be brought back to God and Israel will not be gathered? So it proved; but this is a satisfaction in that case, (1.) Christ will be glorious in the eyes of the Lord; and those are truly glorious that are so in God's eyes. Though few of the Jewish nation were converted by Christ's preaching and miracles, and many of them loaded him with ignominy and disgrace, yet God put honour upon him, and made him glorious, at his baptism, and in his transfiguration, spoke to him from heaven, sent angels to minister to him, made even his shameful death glorious by the many prodigies that attended it, much more his resurrection. Faithful ministers, though they see not the fruit of their labours, shall yet be accepted of God, and in that they shall be truly glorious, for his favour is our honour; and they shall be assisted to proceed and persevere in their labours notwithstanding. This weakens their hands, but their God will be their strength. (2.) The gospel shall be glorious in the eyes of the world; though it be not so in the eyes of the Jews, yet it shall be entertained by the nations, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">v. 6</reference>. The Messiah seemed as if he had been primarily designed to <hi type="italic">bring Jacob back,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">v. 5</reference>. But he is here told that it is comparatively but a small matter; a higher orb of honour than that, and a larger sphere of usefulness, are designed him: "<hi type="italic">It is a light thing that thou shouldst be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob</hi> to the dignity and dominion they expect by the Messiah, and to <hi type="italic">restore the preserved of Israel,</hi> and make them a flourishing church and state as formerly" (nay, considering what a little handful of people they are, it would be but a small matter, in comparison, for the Messiah to be the Saviour of them only); "and therefore <hi type="italic">I will give thee for a light to the Gentiles</hi> (many great and mighty nations by the gospel of Christ shall be brought to the knowledge and worship of the true God), <hi type="italic">that thou mayest be my salvation,</hi> the author of that salvation which I have designed for lost man, and this <hi type="italic">to the end of the earth,</hi> to nations at the greatest distance." Hence Simeon learned to call Christ <hi type="italic">a light to lighten the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Luke ii. 32</reference>), and St. Paul's exposition of this text is what we ought to abide by, and it serves for a key to the context, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">Acts xiii. 47</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> says he, we turn to the Gentiles, to preach the gospel to them, <hi type="italic">because so has the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light to the Gentiles.</hi> In this the Redeemer was truly glorious, though Israel was not gathered; the setting up of his kingdom in the Gentile world was more his honour than if he had raised up all the tribes of Jacob. God had appointed him and set him apart for it: The Lord has called me from the womb to this office and made mention of my name, nominated me to be the Saviour. By an angel he called him Jesus—a Saviour, who should save his people from their sins, Matt. i. 21 . Nay, from the womb of the divine counsels, before all worlds, he was called to this service, and help was laid upon him; and he came at the call, for he said, Lo, I come, with an eye to what was written of him in the volume of the book. God had preferred him to the service for which he had reserved him: He has hidden me in the shadow of his hand and in his quiver, which denotes, (1.) Concealment. The gospel of Christ, and the calling in of the Gentiles by it, were long hidden from ages and generations, hidden in God ( Eph. iii. 5 , Rom. xvi. 25 ), hidden in the shadow of the ceremonial law and the Old-Testament types. (2.) Protection. The house of David was the particular care of the divine Providence, because that blessing was in it. Christ in his infancy was sheltered from the rage of Herod. 4. God had owned him, had said unto him, " Thou art my servant, whom I have employed and will prosper; thou art Israel, in effect, the prince with God, that hast wrestled and prevailed; and in thee I will be glorified." Therefore, says he, we turn to the Gentiles, to preach the gospel to them, because so has the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light to the Gentiles. In this the Redeemer was truly glorious, though Israel was not gathered; the setting up of his kingdom in the Gentile world was more his honour than if he had raised up all the tribes of Jacob. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen16616" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to the Gentiles. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16617" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the Redeemer of Israel, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that is faithful, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages; <hi type="super">9</hi> That thou mayest say to the prisoners, Go forth; to them that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in darkness, Show yourselves. They shall feed in the ways, and their pastures <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in all high places. <hi type="super">10</hi> They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun smite them: for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I will make all my mountains a way, and my highways shall be exalted. <hi type="super">12</hi> Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim. <div eID="gen16617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16618" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen16618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16619" type="x-p"/> I. The humiliation and exaltation of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, and Israel's Holy One,</hi> who had always taken care of the Jewish church and wrought out for them those deliverances that were typical of the great salvation, speaks here to him, who was the undertaker of that salvation. And, 1. He takes notice of his humiliation, the instances of which were uncommon, nay, unparalleled. He was one <hi type="italic">whom man despised.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">despised and rejected of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.3">ch. liii. 3</reference>. To be despised by so mean a creature (man, who is himself a worm) bespeaks the lowest and most contemptible condition imaginable. Man, whom he came to save and to put honour upon, yet despised him and put contempt upon him; so wretchedly ungrateful were his persecutors. The ignominy he underwent was not the least of his sufferings. They not only made him despicable, but odious. He was <hi type="italic">one whom the nation abhorred;</hi> they treated him as the worst of men, and cried out, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi> The nation did it, the Gentiles as well as Jews, and the Jews herein worse than Gentiles; for his cross was <hi type="italic">to the one a stumbling-block</hi> and <hi type="italic">to the other foolishness.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">a servant of rulers;</hi> he was trampled upon, abused, scourged, and crucified as a slave. Pilate boasted of his power over him, <reference osisRef="John.19.10">John xix. 10</reference>. This he submitted to for our salvation. 2. He promises him his exaltation. Honour was done him even in the depth of his humiliation. Herod the king stood in awe of him, saying, <hi type="italic">It is John the Baptist;</hi> noblemen, rulers, centurions came and kneeled to him. But this was more fully accomplished when kings received his gospel, and submitted to his yoke, and joined in the worship of him, and called themselves the vassals of Christ. Not that Christ values the rich more than the poor (they stand upon a level with him), but it is for the honour of his kingdom among men when the great ones of the earth appear for him and do homage to him. This shall be the accomplishment of God's promise, and he will give him the heathen for his inheritance, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> it shall be done, <hi type="italic">because of the Lord who is faithful</hi> and true to his promise; and this shall be an evidence that Christ had a commission for what he did, and that God had chosen him, and would own the choice he had made. <div eID="gen16619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16620" type="x-p"/> II. The blessings he has in store for all those to whom he is made salvation. <div eID="gen16620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> 1. God will own and stand by him in his undertaking (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">In an acceptable time have I heard thee,</hi> that is, I will hear thee. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen16635" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Zion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16636" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Lift up thine eyes round about, and behold: all these gather themselves together, <hi type="italic">and</hi> come to thee. <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou shalt surely clothe thee with them all, as with an ornament, and bind them <hi type="italic">on thee,</hi> as a bride <hi type="italic">doeth.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> For thy waste and thy desolate places, and the land of thy destruction, shall even now be too narrow by reason of the inhabitants, and they that swallowed thee up shall be far away. <hi type="super">20</hi> The children which thou shalt have, after thou hast lost the other, shall say again in thine ears, The place <hi type="italic">is</hi> too strait for me: give place to me that I may dwell. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then shalt thou say in thine heart, Who hath begotten me these, seeing I have lost my children, and am desolate, a captive, and removing to and fro? and who hath brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; these, where <hi type="italic">had</hi> they <hi type="italic">been?</hi> <hi type="super">22</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles, and set up my standard to the people: and they shall bring thy sons in <hi type="italic">their</hi> arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon <hi type="italic">their</hi> shoulders. <hi type="super">23</hi> And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with <hi type="italic">their</hi> face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me. <div eID="gen16636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16637" type="x-p"/> Two things are here promised, which were to be in part accomplished in the reviving of the Jewish church after its return out of captivity, but more fully in the planting of the Christian church by the preaching of the gospel of Christ; and we may take the comfort of these promises. <div eID="gen16637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16638" type="x-p"/> I. That the church shall be replenished with great numbers added to it. It was promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.17">v. 17</reference>) that <hi type="italic">her children should make haste;</hi> that promise is here enlarged upon, and is made very encouraging. It is promised, <div eID="gen16638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16639" type="x-p"/> 1. That multitudes shall flock to the church from all parts. <hi type="italic">Look round, and see how they gather themselves to thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.18">v. 18</reference>), by a local accession to the Jewish church. They come to Jerusalem from all the adjacent countries, for that was then the centre of their unity; but, under the gospel, it is by a spiritual accession to the mystical body of Christ in faith and love. Those that <hi type="italic">come to Jesus as the Mediator of the new covenant</hi> do thereby <hi type="italic">come to the Mount Zion,</hi> the <hi type="italic">church of the first-born,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22-Heb.12.23">Heb. xii. 22, 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lift up thy eyes, and behold</hi> how <hi type="italic">the fields are white unto the harvest,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.35">John iv. 35</reference>. Note, It is matter of joy to the church to see a multitude of converts to Christ. <div eID="gen16639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16640" type="x-p"/> 2. That such as are added to the church shall not be a burden and blemish to her, but her strength and ornament. This part of the promise is confirmed with an oath: <hi type="italic">As I live, saith the Lord, thou shalt surely clothe thyself with them all.</hi> The addition of such numbers to the church shall complete her clothing; and, when all that were chosen are effectually called, then the bride, the Lamb's wife, shall have made herself ready, shall be quite dressed, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>. They shall make her to appear comely and considerable; and she shall therefore bind them on with as much care and complacency as a bride does her ornaments. navigation_sections.content_plain: Glorious things had been spoken in the previous chapters concerning the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon; but lest any should think, when it was accomplished, that it looked much greater and brighter in the prophecy than in the performance, and that the return of about 40,000 Jews in a poor condition out of Babylon to Jerusalem was not an event sufficiently answering to the height and grandeur of the expressions used in the prophecy, he here comes to show that the prophecy had a further intention, and was to have its full accomplishment in a redemption that should as far outdo these expressions as the other seemed to come short of them, even the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ, of whom not only Cyrus, who was God's servant in foretelling it, was a type. In this chapter we have, I. The designation of Christ, under the type of Isaiah, to his office as Mediator, ver. 1-3 . II. The assurance given him of the success of his undertaking among the Gentiles, ver. 4-8 . III. The redemption that should be wrought by him, and the progress of that redemption, ver. 9-12 . IV. The encouragement given hence to the afflicted church, ver. 13-17 . V. The addition of many to it, and the setting up of a church among the Gentiles, ver. 18-23 . VI. A ratification of the prophecy of the Jews' release out of Babylon, which was to be the figure and type of all these blessings,, ver. 24-26 . If this chapter be rightly understood, we shall see ourselves to be more concerned in the prophecies relating to the Jews' deliverance out of Babylon than we thought we were.
